summary: This RFC registers an extension report type for the Abuse Reporting Format, for reports generated at receipt time about messages that fail email authentication checks.

eli5.summary: If an email fails the identity check, the receiver can send back a standard report about it.

questions: what is an arf auth-failure report
subtitle: A standard report format for telling a sender why one of its messages failed DKIM or SPF checks.

tldr.problem: When a received email fails an authentication check such as DKIM or SPF, the receiver had no standard machine-readable way to tell the sender exactly why it failed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an auth-failure feedback type to the Abuse Reporting Format, plus new header fields such as Auth-Failure, Delivery-Result and DKIM-Domain that describe a single failure.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can send detailed, automatable failure reports, with care taken over forgery, report floods and privacy. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6692 and RFC 9991.

today: RFC 6591 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6692 and RFC 9991. No RFC is listed as obsoleting it.

sections.title: Reporting Authentication Failures
sections.content:
The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF, RFC 5965) is a message format for reporting abuse in the messaging infrastructure, designed so that reports can be generated and consumed automatically. Messages that fail an authentication method such as DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) or the Sender Policy Framework (SPF) are sometimes evidence of abuse, and can be detected and reported by automated means.

RFC 6591 extends ARF so these failures can be reported in detail, including forensic information about why the method failed. It does this by registering an extension report type, and it affects several IANA registries. One report describes a single failure; multiple reports MAY be used for multiple failures of one message.
sections.eli5: If an email's identity check fails, the receiver can send back a standard report. That lets the sender figure out what went wrong.

sections.title: The auth-failure Report
sections.content:
The new feedback type is auth-failure. In the second, machine-readable MIME part of the report, several existing ARF fields get stricter rules. Authentication-Results MUST be present and MUST reflect only a single authentication method's result. Original-Envelope-Id, Original-Mail-From and Source-IP are RECOMMENDED where available. Reported-Domain MUST be present if a value is available.

The third MIME part is either message/rfc822 or text/rfc822-headers and holds a copy of the entire header block of the original message. Unlike in the base multipart/report definition, where it is optional, it MUST be included. Report generators may need to redact parts of the message for privacy, and RFC 6590 discusses how.

New fields are grouped by when they apply. Auth-Failure is required in all reports. Delivery-Result is optional, appears at most once, and gives the final disposition: delivered, spam, policy, reject or other.

DKIM reports require DKIM-Domain (from the d= tag), DKIM-Identity (i=) and DKIM-Selector (s=). They may also carry DKIM-Canonicalized-Header and DKIM-Canonicalized-Body, base64 encodings of what the verifier computed. These SHOULD be included unless they would encode redacted data, in which case they MUST NOT be, because altered data would make the comparison useless. ADSP reports require DKIM-ADSP-DNS, and SPF reports require one SPF-DNS field for every SPF record used.
sections.eli5: The report is a form with labeled boxes: what kind of failure, whose signature, and what happened to the email. Some boxes must always be filled and some are optional.

sections.title: Failure Types
sections.content:
The Auth-Failure field takes one of five values, and some of them make other fields mandatory.

  • adsp: the message did not conform to the author domain's published ADSP signing practices. DKIM-ADSP-DNS MUST be included.
  • bodyhash: the body hash in the signature did not match the one computed by the verifier. DKIM-Canonicalized-Body SHOULD be included.
  • revoked: the DKIM key referenced by the signature has been revoked. DKIM-Domain and DKIM-Selector MUST be included.
  • signature: the DKIM signature did not verify against the header hash and public key. DKIM-Domain and DKIM-Selector MUST be included, and DKIM-Canonicalized-Header SHOULD be.
  • spf: evaluating the author domain's SPF record gave none, fail, softfail, temperror or permerror.

The RFC notes that none is not strictly a failure under SPF, but a service that demands successful SPF results could treat it as one. Supplementary data MAY be added as comments, for example to say a message was rejected because it was unsigned when it should have been signed.
sections.eli5: There are five reasons a check can fail, such as a changed message body or a revoked key. Each reason says which extra details must go on the form.

sections.title: Syntax and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Section 4 gives ABNF for the new fields. For example, the Auth-Failure: value is one of adsp, bodyhash, revoked, signature or spf, and SPF-DNS carries a record type (txt or spf), the domain it was retrieved from, and the record content as a quoted string.

IANA considerations add the feedback type auth-failure (email authentication failure report) to the Feedback Report Type Values registry. They also add ten header fields to the Feedback Report Header Fields registry, none of which may appear more than once: Auth-Failure, Delivery-Result, DKIM-ADSP-DNS, DKIM-Canonicalized-Body, DKIM-Canonicalized-Header, DKIM-Domain, DKIM-Identity, DKIM-Selector, DKIM-Selector-DNS and SPF-DNS. Each is related to the feedback type auth-failure and has status current.
sections.eli5: The rules for writing the boxes are spelled out exactly, and the new names are added to the official list so everyone uses them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says these reports raise issues similar to delivery status notifications, and tells implementers to also read the security sections of DKIM, ADSP, SPF and ARF.

Forgery. Reports can be forged as easily as ordinary email, for example by falsely claiming a delivered message failed, or by faking selector and domain details. Signing the reports with DKIM is suggested as a mitigation, but if the verifier's DKIM infrastructure is broken, signed failure reports might not be trusted or accepted.

Floods. Automatic generation can become a denial-of-service source when many messages fail authentication, and an attacker could forge many messages to trigger reports at a victim. Rate limiting helps but may suppress useful information. The RFC suggests generating these reports only after an out-of-band arrangement between two parties, and notes that sending periodic summaries gives up per-incident detail. Report construction should also avoid amplification attacks.

Privacy. Returning canonicalized header and body without redaction is needed so the signer can compare them, but unredacted data can leak information the reporter considers private. For this reason returning them is not required.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake report, and a flood of reports can swamp a mailbox. So it is wise to send reports only to partners who agreed to get them.

items.text: SPF evaluation gave none, fail, softfail, temperror or permerror.
